cards.explanation: The answer is Shechem. Joshua assembles all the tribes there, plus the elders, leaders, judges and officers. That's a guest list that would make me hide my cookie boxes. Keep the name in your pocket, friends, because Shechem shows up again at the very end of this chapter.

The answer is True. Joshua summoned the elders, leaders, judges and officers, and the text says, "…and they presented themselves before God." The tribes and their leaders are standing before Him at Shechem. I'd have checked my apron for flour first.

The answer is False, and that's the honest truth. The LORD says Israel's fathers, including Terah, the father of Abraham and Nahor, lived beyond the Euphrates and worshiped other gods. He doesn't dress up where the family started. He just tells it straight, and that sets up everything else He says.

The answer is Isaac! The LORD says, "I gave him Isaac…" Abraham already had a son Ishmael (Genesis 16:15), so Isaac isn't his first child. But Isaac is the one the LORD names here, and He calls him a gift He gave.

Jacob goes in the first blank. The LORD says, "…to Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau." Two brothers, two paths. Esau got Mount Seir, and Jacob's line is the one this story follows. Egypt goes in the second blank, because the text says Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt, and the LORD brings them back out of it in the next verse.

The answer is False. The text says Israel's fathers cried out to the LORD. Then He put darkness between them and the Egyptians, and brought the sea over the Egyptians. The crying out was theirs, friends, and the rest was the LORD's doing.

The answer is darkness. The LORD put darkness between Israel and the Egyptians. I know a little about darkness myself, from years stuck in the back of a junk drawer. But this was the LORD placing it between the camp of Egypt and the camp of Israel (Exodus 14:20).
The answer is curse. Balak sends for Balaam son of Beor to curse Israel. He wants words that work against them. The text tells us what Balak sent for, and in a moment we find out what he got.

The answer is False! The LORD says, "…I would not listen to Balaam. So he blessed you again and again, and I delivered you from his hand." Balak sent for Balaam to curse Israel and got blessings instead. That's like hiring a guy to boo your rival and watching him lead the cheering.

The answer is that the LORD delivers them into Israel's hand. The people of Jericho fought Israel, and so did the Amorites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hittites, Girgashites, Hivites and Jebusites. The LORD says, "…I delivered them into your hand…" That's a long list of opponents with one ending.

The answer is False. The LORD says, "I sent the hornet ahead of you, and it drove out the two Amorite kings before you, but not by your own sword or bow." So Israel wasn't the one swinging the win into place. He's making sure they know where it came from.

The answer is the gods their fathers served. Joshua says to "cast aside the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt, and serve the LORD." He's telling them to throw out those old gods and serve only the LORD. That's a clean break, friends, and he asks for it right after saying to serve Him in sincerity and truth.
The answer is "We will serve the LORD." Joshua says, "As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!" He says it right after laying out the choice. He doesn't hide where he stands, and I love that.

The answer is that He protected them throughout their journey. The people say, "He also protected us throughout our journey and among all the nations through which we traveled." They look back and see the LORD with them all along the road. That's a pretty solid reason to stick with Him.

The answer is "You are not able to serve the LORD." Joshua says, "You are not able to serve the LORD…" and he says it right after their big promise. Then he gives his reason: "…for He is a holy God; He is a jealous God…" I think Joshua wants them to feel how serious this promise is.

The answer is False. The people reply, "No!" and then, "…we will serve the LORD!" Joshua tells them they can't, and they say it again anyway. That's like a baker who hears "too hot" and grabs the oven mitts.

The answer is witnesses. Joshua says, "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen to serve the LORD." Their own words are on the record, and they're the ones who said them. It's like signing your own name on the cookie box.
The answer is False. The people don't refuse, they agree. Joshua says, "You are witnesses against yourselves…" and the people reply, "We are witnesses!" That's a yes to their own promise.

The answer is that they will serve the LORD and obey His voice. The people say, "We will serve the LORD our God and obey His voice." Notice the new part, friends, obeying His voice. Joshua told them to get rid of the foreign gods and incline their hearts, and this is their answer.
The answer is stone. Joshua takes a large stone and sets it up under the oak near the sanctuary of the LORD. It gives the people something they can see. Next, he tells them what that rock is for.

The answer is that it has heard all the LORD's words to them. Joshua says, "You see this stone. It will be a witness against us, for it has heard all the words the LORD has spoken to us…" That's his reason. Anyone can walk up and look at it, and it stands there as a reminder.

The answer is 110. Joshua son of Nun died at the age of 110, and the text calls him "…the servant of the LORD…" right where it tells of his death. I think that's a title worth having on the last page.

The answer is True. The text says, "Israel had served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him and who had experienced all the works that the LORD had done for Israel." It names two stretches: Joshua's days, and the days of those elders. The promise at Shechem held that long.
